pointers.sentence: With `"pool"` in an alias's `"OPTIONS"`, the `pool` property makes one pool for the alias (Oracle's, for the alias and its `"USER"`), and `get_new_connection` takes each connection from it (`django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.pool`, `django/db/backends/oracle/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.pool`).

With `"pool"` in an alias's `"OPTIONS"`, the `pool` property makes one pool for the alias (Oracle's, for the alias and its `"USER"`), and `get_new_connection` takes each connection from it (`django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.pool`, `django/db/backends/oracle/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.pool`).

The 5.1 notes' reason: opening a connection can take relatively long, and keeping connections open can reduce latency (`docs/releases/5.1.txt`; [Opening and closing a connection](../backends/lifecycle.md#connection-pools-postgresql-and-oracle)).
Since 5.1 SQLite's backend takes two keys out of `"OPTIONS"` (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.get_connection_params`).

Since 5.2 MySQL's backend asks for the character set `"utf8mb4"`, where it asked for `"utf8"`, which the notes call an alias of the deprecated `"utf8mb3"`; a `"charset"` in `"OPTIONS"` still replaces it (`django/db/backends/mysql/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.get_connection_params`; [MySQL and MariaDB](../backends/mysql.md#the-driver-mysqldb-and-opening-a-connection)).

5.0 added oracledb to Oracle's backend and deprecated cx_Oracle, which 6.0 removed: at this commit the backend imports oracledb alone (`django/db/backends/oracle/base.py`; [Oracle](../backends/oracle.md#the-driver-and-the-processs-environment)).

Since 5.0 a `django.db.models.UUIDField` on MariaDB is a column of the type `"uuid"`, where it was `"char(32)"`, as MySQL's still is; the 5.0 notes ask that a field made before then be replaced by a subclass backed by `"char(32)"` (`django/db/backends/mysql/base.py:DatabaseWrapper.data_types`).

The 5.0 notes say MariaDB 10.7 and later; at this commit the flag asks only whether the server is MariaDB (`django/db/backends/mysql/features.py:DatabaseFeatures.has_native_uuid_field`; [Column types: from a field to a column](../backends/column-types.md#mysqls-two-properties)).

Since 5.0 SQLite's operations give every integer field a 64-bit range, "to match the behavior of sqlite3", the notes say, and the validators of an integer field read it, so on SQLite a `SmallIntegerField` is validated up to 9223372036854775807 (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/operations.py:DatabaseOperations.integer_field_range`; [The field classes](../models/field-types.md#integers)).

6.1 added `django.db.transaction.savepoint_create` and deprecated `savepoint`, which now warns and calls it (`django/db/transaction.py:savepoint`; [Transactions: autocommit, `atomic` and savepoints](../backends/transactions.md#savepoints); [What still warns: the deprecations and the releases that end them](deprecations.md)).

5.0 deprecated the operations' method field_cast_sql for `BaseDatabaseOperations.lookup_cast`, and 6.0 removed it: at this commit `BuiltinLookup.process_lhs` asks `lookup_cast` alone (`django/db/models/lookups.py:BuiltinLookup.process_lhs`).

Since 6.1 `DurationField.get_db_prep_value` hands a duration to `BaseDatabaseOperations.adapt_durationfield_value`, whose base gives an integer of microseconds and which PostgreSQL's and Oracle's operations override to pass it through (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:DurationField.get_db_prep_value`).

Since 5.0 the serializer writes a function under `functools.cache` or `functools.lru_cache` by its name, its CPython class being among `FUNCTION_TYPES` (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:FUNCTION_TYPES`; [Serializing values: `serializer_factory` and `deconstruct`](../migrations/serializer.md#the-registry-in-its-order)).

Since 6.0 `ZoneInfoSerializer` writes a `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo`, which 5.2.17 refuses, and a keyword argument of a deconstructed call whose name is not an identifier goes into a dictionary after `**` (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:DeconstructibleSerializer.serialize_deconstructed`).

Since 6.0 a `functools.partial` is written as a deconstructed call, `functools.partial(int, base=2)` where 5.2.17 wrote `functools.partial(int, *(), **{'base': 2})` (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:FunctoolsPartialSerializer`), and `DeconstructibleSerializer` is the name of what was DeconstructableSerializer, with no alias left.
Since 6.1 `GenericAliasSerializer` writes a generic alias such as `list[int]` (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:GenericAliasSerializer`).

Since 5.1 an operation has a category, `Operation.category`, a member of `OperationCategory` whose values are signs: `"+"` an addition, `"-"` a removal, `"~"` an alteration, `"p"` Python, `"s"` SQL, `"?"` a mix. makemigrations prints each operation's sign before its description, `"?"` for the base class's `None` (`django/db/migrations/operations/base.py:Operation.formatted_description`; [Operations: the base class and its two halves](../migrations/operations.md#category-describe-and-the-name-fragment)).

Since 5.2 makemigrations and migrate make their autodetector from a class attribute, which a subclass of the command may replace (`django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py:Command.autodetector`).

Since 5.2 a constraint changed only in what `BaseConstraint.non_db_attrs` names, `"violation_error_code"` and `"violation_error_message"`, becomes an `AlterConstraint`, which changes the state and nothing in the database (`django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector._constraint_should_be_dropped_and_recreated`; [The autodetector: fields, indexes and constraints](../migrations/autodetector-fields.md#constraints-create_altered_constraints)).

Until 6.2 the autodetector kept such a model apart, and wrote for it only its creation, its deletion, and changes to its table's name or comment and to some options; at this commit it compares the model as it does any other (`django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector._detect_changes`).

Such an operation changes the state and no table, since `Operation.allow_migrate_model` refuses a model that cannot be migrated: a schema editor collecting its SQL collects none, under every release (`django/db/migrations/operations/base.py:Operation.allow_migrate_model`; [The autodetector: comparing two project states](../migrations/autodetector.md#detect_changes-the-models-sorted-then-the-generators-in-order)).

The loader follows such a chain down to the migrations that replace nothing, whose rows decide whether it counts as applied, and refuses a cycle (`django/db/migrations/loader.py:MigrationLoader.replace_migration`; [Squashed migrations: `replaces` and the squashmigrations command](../migrations/squashing.md#a-replacing-migration-that-is-replaced)).
